suite.doc: Homa works end to end: jumbo frames through sw1, a Homa round trip between every pair of hosts over IPv4 and IPv6 (contents validated by the echo servers), message sizes from 8 bytes (the echo protocol's own header: the second word is the reply length) to Homa's 1 MB maximum, and the module's lifecycle (it refuses to unload while sockets are open, unloads, and the kernel loads it again on the first IPPROTO 146 socket).

suite.doc: Incast at h1: h2 and h3 stream 500 KB messages to h1 (twice what h1's 1 Gbit/s port at sw1 can take) while h4 sends 100 B probes to h1, one at a time, to separate server processes. Once with sw1's strict priority queues, once with one FIFO queue; Homa, then TCP. Homa's short messages go at the top priority, so with priority queues they pass the bulk data queued at the bottleneck — the effect Homa is designed around. TCP marks everything priority 0 and gets no such help.

suite.doc: A finding of this lab, kept as a test. Two senders push 500 KB messages into h1's 1 Gbit/s port. Homa's SRPT grants put the message nearest completion at the top scheduled priority and park the others at lower ones, which strict priority queues then starve for many milliseconds. Homa's resend timer (resend_ticks = 5 ms of silence) assumes a 25-100 Gbit/s network where that never lasts so long: the receiver asks for data that is only queued, the sender sends it again into the same starved queue, and sw1 overflows and RPCs time out. Scaled to this link speed (x10) the spurious RESENDs mostly vanish.
